..
Issued at 151 PM CDT Sat Jul 25 2026

Low-level moisture will work its way northward across the region  
this evening and tonight. At the same time, the eastern 
periphery of an advancing EML plume will push across the 
Mississippi River early Sunday morning. There has been a modest 
increase in the signal this morning for elevated convective 
development along the fringes of this EML plume overnight into 
Sunday morning as persistent but modest warm advection/upglide 
works to lift and moisten the base of this conditionally 
unstable layer. Definitely not a ubiquitous signal, but 
certainly enough to justify an inclusion of some slight chance 
PoPs in the vicinity of our I-39 locales through mid-late 
morning. If this activity does materialize, elevated storms 
would be capable of producing a few instances of severe hail. 
Finally, an intense MCS is forecast to develop this evening and 
roll across parts of South Dakota. This feature should begin to
weaken across central and eastern Iowa as it encounters stronger
capping. If it manages to persist longer than expected, 850-300
mb thicknesses and the MUCAPE orientation suggest the complex 
should still remain mostly south and west of the area, but the 
slight chance PoPs also cover the low potential for outflow and 
lingering convection getting close to the CWA. 

Air temperatures on Sunday are largely expected to top out in
the upper 80s to low 90s. The mid/upper 90s on the HRRR are 
likely overdone due to an overmixed boundary layer. Dewpoints 
are forecast to range from the low/mid 70s across the eastern 
half of the CWA and into the upper 70s farther west, locally 
higher near agricultural areas. Resultant peak heat indices are 
expected to range from the mid/upper 90s near the lake to 
locally around 105 in our far west/southwest locales in the 
vicinity of the I-39 corridor. There is some potential that 
convective debris muddies up the temperature forecast a bit near
the I-39 corridor, but close enough that we'll hoist targeted 
Advisory for our far western counties. 

For Sunday afternoon and evening: most guidance shows fairly
strong capping in place across our forecast area. The one 
exception will be closer to the Mississippi River where upper 
70s and lower 80 degree dewpoints will be present which may lead
to a local minima in MLCIN. Anything from lingering convection,
to a convectively-augmented MCV, to subtle vort maxes embedded 
within the northwesterly flow aloft could serve as the focus for
additional development late in the afternoon/early evening. Any
activity would pose a severe risk given modest deep layer shear
(35-40 kts) and the very large instability reservoir. Suppose 
the lake breeze across eastern Wisconson could also serve as a 
surface focus, but at present, capping seems to preclude this as
a more likely scenario, at least through the early evening. 
Still seeing a signal for perhaps more widespread convective 
coverage materializing late Sunday evening and overnight to our 
north and then pushing south down the instability gradient and 
will continue to carry chance PoPs for this possibility. As 
before, any thunderstorms during this period may be strong to 
severe. 

Monday's forecast remains highly uncertain. Any number of
remnant subtle forcing mechanisms along the periphery of a more
notable shortwave trough scooting across the UP of Michigan 
could serve as foci for additional storm development through the
morning and afternoon. Forecast outcomes continue to range from
little/no storm coverage locally (focused mainly to the east), 
to one or two MCSs dropping south across the area, to semi-
discrete supercell development on or ahead of an incoming front
during the afternoon and evening. No changes to the NBM- 
delivered PoPs at this time, which show a SW-NE gradient in 
chances across the area (highest the farther east you go) which 
seems appropriate given today's model guidance. 

In an undisturbed airmass, fairly widespread heat indices of
105+ are in play on Monday, locally towards 110 where ET 
effects are most pronounced. However, any morning/early 
afternoon MCS activity/outflow have the potential to greatly 
impact these values. Chances for widespread 110+ peak heat 
indices still seem pretty low even in the scenario with no 
storms, and likely confined to our far southwest counties. As a 
result, continue to hold off on any heat headlines for Monday. 

A cold front will shift through the region late Monday night 
into early Tuesday morning. Onshore flow will hold lakeside 
temperatures in the upper 70s to near 80 degrees Tuesday through
Thursday, and conditions will turn less humid. Looks like a 
strong push of northerly winds will accompany the front, which 
will lead to building wave action and likely a high swim/rip 
current risk Tuesday through Wednesday. Generally dry/precip- 
free conditions are expected through the end of the week with 
high pressure back in control. 

Carlaw
